newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan seals off gunman's village after protests.
newsitem.headline: Jordan seals off gunman's village after protests.

text.p: Jordanian police sealed off on Wednesday the village of a soldier who killed seven Israeli schoolgirls and residents said 28 people who marched to protest his life sentence had been detained.

Police turned cars away from the northern village of Ibdr and an army jeep patrolled its streets after Tuesday's show of support for private Ahmed Daqamsa, who shot the girls on a visit to the Jordanian border in March.
Villagers said those still being held included Daqamsa's mother, sister and other relatives.
Protestors carrying banners, Korans and a picture of Daqamsa clashed with police on Tuesday as they marched out of Ibdr calling for his sentence of hard labour for life to be reduced.
Police used teargas and batons to disperse the mostly women marchers and brought in reinforcements by helicopter after people set fire to tyres on the road, the villagers said.
Daqamsa's attack on the girls four months ago shook Jordan.

King Hussein condemned it as a shameful and cowardly act but opponents of his 1994 peace treaty with Israel rushed to defend Daqamsa, portraying him variously as a patriot, victim of mental illness, or a pawn in Jordan's ties with the Jewish state.
An army tribunal ruled on Saturday that Daqamsa was incapable of a premeditated crime but said he shot the schoolgirls, aged 11 to 13, deliberately and unprovoked.
Daqamsa's family said military judges should have been more lenient on a man with a history of mental disorder.

"We ask the king to ease his sentence," Daqamsa's wife Fatima told Reuters. "We ask for Ahmed to be considered the same way that the Israelis considered the soldier who opened fire in Hebron. He was released because he was mad."
Israeli soldier Naom Friedman who fired on Palestinians in the West Bank town of Hebron in January was sent to a psychiatric hospital instead of facing charges.

"Israelis kill in Lebanon and the West Bank every day, with no punishment," said one of Daqamsa's relatives who asked not to be identified. He said Daqamsa's village of 2,000 people was being punished collectively for the shooting.

Daqamsa's family attended his two month trial outside Amman but were barred from travelling south to the court on the two days when Israeli witnesses, making their first appearance in a Jordanian courtroom, testified against him.
They said drivers were told they faced 800 dinar ($1,130) fines and two weeks in jail if they took his family to Amman.
The Israelis were invited to dinner with the king.
"They want to arrest all the Daqamsas but we will not be silenced -- either over the sentence or by this state terrorism," said another relative who asked not to be identified.

The hilltop village, about 20 km (12 miles) east of the Israeli border, was accessible by foot but villagers said police blocking its only access road had a list of people wanted over Tuesday's protest.
